A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same metabench research, using the same six source benchmarks and LLM response corpus. Text, equations, tables, figures and appendices are readable, and retained material can be matched across substantial reorganization.

before.justification: V1 reports original analyses of LLM responses, including held-out score reconstruction, comparisons with random subsets, factor analysis and adaptive-testing simulations.

after.justification: V2 retains original empirical analyses and adds dimensionality and selection comparisons, synthetic simulations, seed sensitivity, architecture-specific errors and LLM fine-tuning experiments.

M1.justification: V1 reconstructs scores from latent abilities. V2 adds subtest scores and, for joint prediction, weighted linear predictions from item responses and aggregate predictors (Section 2.3; Appendix B.5). These change the reconstruction procedure substantially. V2 also introduces disjoint benchmark forms and optional answer-choice permutation for repeated evaluation.

E1.justification: The six real benchmarks and original response corpus remain. Coverage expands through synthetic paired benchmarks with controlled ability overlap (B.6) and deliberate memorization and answer-permutation scenarios (Section 3.2). The second disjoint form uses existing benchmark coverage rather than adding another substantive domain.

E2.justification: V2 adds a direct k-means item-selection comparator within the metabench pipeline across all six benchmarks and their aggregate (B.8, Table 6). It also compares one- versus two-dimensional IRT models and expands CAT estimator and selection comparisons. Random subsampling and logistic-regression comparisons from v1 remain.

E3.justification: The primary selected set changes from 739 to 858 items, with revised IRT configurations. Table 1's stated correlation target changes from latent abilities versus original scores to predicted versus true scores. Main CAT evaluation shifts from training-set ability RMSE to held-out benchmark-score RMSE, alongside a new 40-model configuration sweep. The original stratified split scheme remains.

E4.justification: V2 adds controlled synergy simulations, dimensionality and clustering ablations, agreement between disjoint forms, seed sensitivity and architecture-conditioned error analysis (B.6-B.12). Section 3.2 tests memorization mitigation through fine-tuning and answer permutation. CAT gains parameter sensitivity and item-count/error analyses; these extend the earlier simulations substantively.

E5.justification: V2 newly reports running the entire distillation pipeline with five seeds, displaying individual outcomes and means in Figure 9. It also averages synergy simulations over five seeds and describes nonparametric reconstruction confidence intervals in Section 3.1. V1's 10,000 random-subset comparisons did not provide these uncertainty assessments.

E6.justification: Primary joint reconstruction results change from mean benchmark RMSE 1.508% and aggregate RMSE 0.814% to 1.24% and 0.582% (Section 2.5; Table 2). Predictors and item sets also change, so these are not identical-setting gains. V2 reports a 751-item secondary form with aggregate RMSE 0.675%, plus new ablation, memorization, stability and CAT score-recovery results.

T1.justification: The core IRT likelihood, Fisher-information expression and factor-analysis derivations remain. Appendix B.5 adds formal definitions of the expanded reconstruction models and weighted-response predictors. V1 Appendix D's infit/outfit definitions are omitted. These are limited changes to mathematical content, without a new theorem or proof.

C1.justification: The central claims of sparse six-benchmark evaluation and a common latent factor remain. V2 adds repeated-evaluation use, specifies reasoning and knowledge in the title and conclusion, and strengthens its advertised reconstruction accuracy. Section 1.1 also newly claims to halve errors reported by tinyBenchmarks.

C2.justification: V2 adds substantive discussion of contamination and its assumed stability across evaluated models, explains when cross-benchmark synergy helps, and distinguishes predictive dimensionality from the number of underlying abilities. CAT conclusions become more qualified: general superiority over fixed metabench is not established, and premature confidence can cause poor score recovery (Appendix C.3).

D1.justification: V2 reports HuggingFace hosting, evaluation-harness integration, the reconstruct.R workflow, available fitted models and Zenodo data access (Sections 3.1 and 4.4). It adds predictor specifications, fine-tuning tooling and CAT numerical-integration settings. Documentation also loses some precision: v1's exact part-whole correlation filtering cutoffs are no longer stated.

R1.justification: Section 1.1 adds substantive comparison with BenchBuilder and expands the brief tinyBenchmarks discussion into explicit arguments about model fitting, item selection, latent abilities and performance. Additional literature supports multidimensional estimation, contamination and CAT alternatives. This substantially revises the positioning relative to nearby research.

P1.justification: V2 reorganizes the narrative around a new usage section, restructures related work, condenses the conclusion and adds ethics and reproducibility statements. Main-text adaptive testing and its procedural appendix are consolidated into Appendix C, while factor analysis moves to D. Terminology, captions and explanatory passages are extensively revised.

P2.justification: The pipeline and headline-results figures exchange positions and are resized; table headings and comparison indicators change. V1's 350-item reconstruction figure is omitted, while v2 adds synergy, form-agreement, seed, architecture and CAT-error plots. MAE and CAT tables are substantially expanded, alongside conversion to the ICLR layout.

improvement.justification: V1 left important questions about selection alternatives, seed sensitivity and memorization largely untested. V2 addresses these with targeted experiments, provides a usable evaluation workflow and qualifies CAT claims using held-out score recovery. These substantially strengthen evidential support and practical usefulness. The larger item budget and reporting inconsistencies, including incorrect differences in Table 6, temper the accuracy claims but do not outweigh these gains.
